Urban farming, as the name suggests, refers to growing vegetables, fruit and herbs within a city, on rooftops, on balconies, in abandoned factories, or even on the walls of buildings.
In the past, cities and farmland were clearly separated. Food was produced in the countryside and transported hundreds or even thousands of kilometres to reach the dinner tables of city residents. This long journey not only consumes a great deal of energy but also means that vegetables are often harvested before they are fully ripe, and a considerable portion is wasted on the way. As the urban population continues to grow, how to feed cities in a more sustainable way has become a pressing question.
Urban farming offers one possible answer. First, it shortens the distance between the field and the table, so that residents can eat vegetables picked on the same day. Second, green roofs can lower the temperature of buildings in summer and absorb rainwater during storms. Third, community gardens give neighbours who seldom talk to each other a reason to work side by side.
Of course, urban farms cannot replace traditional agriculture. Land in cities is expensive, and staple crops such as rice and wheat still require vast fields. However, as a supplement, urban farming allows people who have grown up surrounded by concrete to rediscover where their food comes from.

城市农业，顾名思义，是指在城市里，在屋顶、阳台、废弃的工厂，甚至建筑物的墙面上种植蔬菜、水果和香草。
过去，城市与农田界限分明。粮食在乡村生产出来，要经过成百上千公里的运输，才能到达城市居民的餐桌。这段漫长的旅程不仅消耗大量的能源，还意味着蔬菜往往没有完全成熟就被采摘，并且有相当一部分在途中被浪费掉。随着城市人口不断增长，如何以更可持续的方式养活城市，已成为一个紧迫的问题。
城市农业提供了一种可能的答案。首先，它缩短了从田间到餐桌的距离，居民可以吃到当天采摘的蔬菜。其次，绿色屋顶能在夏季降低建筑物的温度，在暴雨时吸收雨水。再次，社区菜园让平时很少交谈的邻居有了并肩劳动的理由。
当然，城市农场无法取代传统农业。城市的土地价格昂贵，水稻、小麦这样的主粮仍然需要广阔的田地。但是作为一种补充，城市农业让那些在钢筋水泥中长大的人重新认识到，自己的食物是从哪里来的。

Sleep, in simple terms, is a state in which the body rests while the brain remains surprisingly busy.
For a long time, people regarded sleep as a waste of time. Some famous figures even boasted that they needed only four hours a night. In modern society, with the spread of electric light and, more recently, smartphones, the hours people spend asleep have been steadily shrinking. Many office workers stay up late to finish their tasks, and students sacrifice sleep to prepare for examinations, believing that this is the price of success.
Scientists, however, have reached a very different conclusion. During sleep, the brain sorts through the information collected during the day, strengthening useful memories and discarding what is unnecessary. At the same time, it clears away the waste products that have built up while we are awake. People who sleep less than six hours a night for a long period not only find it harder to concentrate but also face a higher risk of heart disease and depression.
Therefore, sleep should not be seen as the enemy of efficiency. On the contrary, it is the foundation of it. A person who has slept well can often complete in one hour what a tired person cannot finish in three. Instead of asking how little sleep we can survive on, perhaps we should ask how we can protect the sleep we need.

简单地说，睡眠是这样一种状态：身体在休息，大脑却出人意料地忙碌着。
很长一段时间里，人们把睡眠看作对时间的浪费。一些名人甚至夸耀自己每晚只需要睡四个小时。在现代社会，随着电灯的普及，以及近年来智能手机的普及，人们的睡眠时间一直在不断缩短。许多上班族熬夜完成任务，学生牺牲睡眠来备考，他们相信这是成功必须付出的代价。
然而，科学家得出了截然不同的结论。在睡眠中，大脑会整理白天收集到的信息，巩固有用的记忆，丢弃不需要的内容。与此同时，它还会清除我们清醒时积累下来的代谢废物。长期每晚睡眠不足六小时的人，不仅更难集中注意力，患心脏病和抑郁症的风险也更高。
因此，睡眠不应被视为效率的敌人，恰恰相反，它是效率的基础。一个睡得好的人，往往一个小时就能完成一个疲惫的人三个小时也做不完的事。与其问我们最少睡多久就能撑下去，或许我们更应该问，怎样才能保护好我们所需要的睡眠。

A "slow city", literally understood, is a city that chooses to live at a slower pace.
The idea was born in a small Italian town in 1999. At that time, fast food chains and large supermarkets were spreading rapidly, and many old shops and local traditions were disappearing. The mayor and several of his colleagues worried that their town would soon look exactly like everywhere else. They proposed a different path: instead of chasing speed and scale, a town should protect its own character and the quality of life of its residents.
To be recognised as a slow city, a town must meet a series of requirements. Its population should not exceed fifty thousand. It should limit traffic and noise in the centre, support local farmers and craftsmen, preserve historic buildings, and reduce the use of neon signs. There should be more squares and green spaces where people can sit and talk, and fewer cars rushing by.
Some critics argue that this is merely a romantic dream which rejects modern life. Supporters reply that being slow does not mean being backward. Slow cities welcome new technology as long as it serves people rather than controls them. What they oppose is not progress but the blind worship of speed. In an age when everyone seems to be in a hurry, they remind us that a good life needs time to be tasted.

“慢城”，从字面上理解，就是选择以较慢的节奏生活的城市。
这一理念于1999年诞生在意大利的一个小镇。当时，快餐连锁店和大型超市迅速扩张，许多老店铺和地方传统正在消失。镇长和他的几位同事担心，自己的小镇很快就会变得与别的地方一模一样。他们提出了一条不同的道路：一座城镇不应追逐速度和规模，而应保护自身的特色和居民的生活质量。
要被认定为慢城，一座城镇必须满足一系列要求。它的人口不得超过五万；应当限制市中心的交通和噪声，扶持本地的农民和手工艺人，保护历史建筑，减少霓虹灯招牌的使用；应当有更多可供人们坐下来聊天的广场和绿地，少一些飞驰而过的汽车。
一些批评者认为，这不过是一个拒绝现代生活的浪漫梦想。支持者则回应说，慢并不意味着落后。只要新技术是为人服务而不是控制人，慢城同样欢迎它。他们反对的不是进步，而是对速度的盲目崇拜。在一个人人似乎都行色匆匆的时代，他们提醒我们，美好的生活需要时间去品味。

Lifelong learning, as the term implies, means that education does not end when a person leaves school but continues throughout one's entire life.
In the past, a person's life was usually divided into three clear stages: studying in youth, working in middle age, and resting in old age. The knowledge acquired at school was generally enough for a whole career. A carpenter or a doctor could rely on the skills learned in his twenties until retirement.
Today this pattern has been broken. With the rapid progress of technology, the knowledge in many fields becomes outdated within a few years. Some jobs disappear, while new ones that nobody had heard of a decade ago are created. A person who stops learning after graduation may soon find that he can no longer keep up with his own profession.
Fortunately, learning has never been so convenient. Online courses allow people to attend lectures given by famous professors without leaving home, and many universities have opened evening classes for working adults. In some countries, elderly people return to the classroom to study painting, history or foreign languages, not for a diploma but for the pleasure of learning itself.
Lifelong learning, therefore, is not merely a way to avoid being eliminated. More importantly, it keeps the mind active and gives people the courage to face a changing world.

终身学习，顾名思义，是指教育并不在一个人离开学校时结束，而是贯穿人的一生。
过去，人的一生通常被分为三个清晰的阶段：年轻时读书，中年时工作，年老时休息。在学校里学到的知识，一般足够用上整个职业生涯。一名木匠或一名医生，可以凭着二十多岁时学到的本领一直干到退休。
如今，这种模式已被打破。随着技术的飞速进步，许多领域的知识在几年之内就会过时。一些工作消失了，另一些十年前闻所未闻的新工作又被创造出来。一个毕业后就停止学习的人，可能很快就会发现自己跟不上本行业的发展了。
幸运的是，学习从未像今天这样方便。网络课程让人们足不出户就能听到著名教授的讲课，许多大学也为在职的成年人开设了夜校。在一些国家，老年人重返课堂，学习绘画、历史或外语，不是为了一纸文凭，而是为了享受学习本身的乐趣。
因此，终身学习不仅仅是避免被淘汰的手段。更重要的是，它使头脑保持活跃，给人们以面对变化中的世界的勇气。

Light pollution, in plain words, is the excessive or misdirected artificial light produced by human activities at night.
For most of human history, the night was truly dark. People planned their journeys according to the moon and told stories under a sky crowded with stars. Since the invention of the electric lamp, however, cities have grown brighter and brighter. Street lamps, advertising boards and the illuminated outer walls of skyscrapers have turned night into day. It is estimated that more than a third of the world's population can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live.
The loss is not only an aesthetic one. Too much light at night disturbs the internal clock of the human body and makes it difficult to fall asleep. Wild animals suffer even more. Migrating birds, which rely on starlight to find their way, are confused by the glow of cities and crash into tall buildings. Newly hatched sea turtles crawl towards streetlights instead of the sea.
Fortunately, light pollution is one of the easiest kinds of pollution to reduce. Unlike polluted water or soil, darkness returns the moment a lamp is switched off. Installing shades so that lamps shine only downwards and turning off decorative lighting after midnight can make a great difference. Some regions have even set up dark-sky reserves, so that children can once again look up and see the stars.

光污染，通俗地说，就是人类夜间活动所产生的过量的或者照射方向不当的人造光。
在人类历史的大部分时间里，夜晚是真正黑暗的。人们根据月亮来安排行程，在繁星密布的天空下讲故事。然而自从电灯发明以来，城市变得越来越亮。路灯、广告牌和摩天大楼被照亮的外墙，把黑夜变成了白昼。据估计，全世界有三分之一以上的人在自己居住的地方已经看不到银河了。
这种损失不仅仅是审美上的。夜间过多的光线会扰乱人体的生物钟，使人难以入睡。野生动物受到的伤害更大。依靠星光辨别方向的候鸟被城市的光芒弄得晕头转向，撞上高楼；刚孵出的小海龟不是爬向大海，而是爬向路灯。
幸运的是，光污染是最容易减少的污染之一。与被污染的水或土壤不同，灯一关，黑暗立刻就回来了。给灯加装灯罩，使它只向下照射，午夜以后关闭装饰性的照明，就能带来很大的改变。一些地区甚至设立了暗夜保护区，让孩子们能够再次抬头看见星星。
